original_question: Find the asymptotic value of D_d(n), where D_d(n) is the minimum number of distinct distances that an n-point set in R^d can determine.
target_in_paper: Section 4 (Higher dimensions), Problem 10: Find the asymptotic value of D_d(n), after the paper defines D_d(n) and discusses the lattice upper bound and Theorem 4.1.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's actual target. It uses the paper's notation D_d(n), places the problem in R^d, and asks for the asymptotic behavior of the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point set.
missing_details: The paper's D_d(n) is defined using ordinary Euclidean distances in R^d.
The minimum is taken over all point sets P subset of R^d with |P| = n, and the distances counted are those determined by pairs of distinct points p, q in P.
The asymptotic question is in the regime n -> infinity with d fixed.
In the paper this is the higher-dimensional variant, so the intended scope is d >= 3; the planar case d = 2 is treated separately earlier in the survey.
The nearby context records the benchmark upper bound D_d(n) = O(n^(2/d)) from the n^(1/d) x ... x n^(1/d) integer lattice and says this is conjectured to be tight for d >= 3.
refined_question: For each fixed integer d >= 3, let D_d(n) be the minimum, over all n-point sets P subset of R^d, of the number of distinct Euclidean distances {||p-q|| : p, q in P, p != q}. Determine the asymptotic order of growth of D_d(n) as n -> infinity.
justification: The draft is targeting the higher-dimensional distinct distances problem in Section 4. There the paper first defines D_d(n) for n-point sets in R^d, then states the lattice-based upper bound D_d(n) = O(n^(2/d)) and notes that this bound is conjectured to be tight for d >= 3, and finally records the official open problem as Problem 10: Find the asymptotic value of D_d(n). So the faithful refinement is not a broader Erdős-distance question, but simply the same problem with the quantifiers, Euclidean metric, fixed-d asymptotic regime, and higher-dimensional scope made explicit.
